subject: Science
name: Science, Year 9
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Stimulus, receptor and effector
points.brief: A stimulus is a change inside or outside the body. Receptors detect it, a control centre such as the brain decides, and effectors such as muscles or glands respond.

points.title: The nervous system
points.brief: Neurons carry fast electrical impulses between receptors, the brain and spinal cord, and effectors. A reflex skips the brain for a faster response.

points.title: The endocrine system
points.brief: Glands release hormones into the blood, which carry messages more slowly than nerves but with longer-lasting effects, such as adrenaline in a fright.

points.title: Negative feedback
points.brief: Negative feedback keeps conditions steady by reversing a change, as sweating cools the body when it gets too hot and shivering warms it when cold.

points.title: Blood glucose and diabetes
points.brief: Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose after a meal. In diabetes this feedback fails, which is why some people need insulin injections.

points.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
points.brief: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and makes identical offspring. Sexual reproduction joins two gametes and makes offspring that vary.

points.title: Gametes and fertilisation
points.brief: Sperm are small and can swim to the egg. The egg is large and holds food for early growth. Fertilisation joins them to start a new organism.

points.title: Reproduction in flowering plants
points.brief: Pollen is carried to the stigma by wind or animals, fertilises an ovule, and the ovule becomes a seed inside a fruit. Many plants also grow new plants from runners or bulbs.

points.title: Why variation helps a species survive
points.brief: Varied offspring make it more likely that some survive a change such as a new disease, while asexual reproduction is faster in a stable place.

points.title: Number of offspring and parental care
points.brief: Animals that care for their young usually have few offspring, while those that give no care, such as many fish, produce huge numbers.

points.title: Earth's four spheres
points.brief: The geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere are the rock, life, water and air of the Earth, and matter and energy move between them.

points.title: Photosynthesis and respiration in the carbon cycle
points.brief: Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air into plants, and respiration by living things returns it.

points.title: Combustion and carbon stores
points.brief: Carbon is stored for long times in fossil fuels, rocks, oceans and forests. Burning fossil fuels releases it quickly as carbon dioxide.

points.title: The greenhouse effect
points.brief: Gases such as carbon dioxide trap some of the heat leaving Earth, which keeps it warm enough for life. More of these gases trap more heat.

points.title: Capturing carbon
points.brief: Forests, soils and oceans take up carbon naturally, and fire management by First Nations Australians and new technologies can help store more.

points.title: Conduction
points.brief: In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle as they collide. Metals conduct heat well, while air and wool are insulators.

points.title: Convection
points.brief: Warm fluid spreads out, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler fluid sinks, setting up a convection current in liquids and gases.

points.title: Sound as a wave
points.brief: Sound is a vibration passed through a medium by particles, so it travels faster in solids than in air and cannot travel through a vacuum.

points.title: Parts of a wave
points.brief: Wavelength is the distance between peaks, amplitude the height of a wave, and frequency the number of waves each second. Higher frequency sounds have a higher pitch.

points.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
points.brief: Light is one part of a family of electromagnetic waves, from radio waves and microwaves through infrared and visible light to ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All travel through a vacuum.

points.title: Wave and particle models of light
points.brief: Light behaves like a wave when it spreads and bends, and like a stream of particles called photons when it is absorbed. Each model explains different things.

points.title: Static and current electricity
points.brief: Static electricity is a build-up of charge on an object. Current electricity is a flow of charge through a conductor, pushed by a voltage.

points.title: Conservation of energy
points.brief: Energy cannot be made or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, so the total energy in a system stays the same.

points.title: Efficiency and Sankey diagrams
points.brief: Efficiency is useful energy out divided by total energy in, as a percentage. A Sankey diagram's arrow widths show where the energy goes.

points.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
points.brief: Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge, and both sit in the nucleus. Electrons are negative, far lighter, and move around it.

points.title: How the model of the atom changed
points.brief: Thomson found the electron, Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed a small dense nucleus, and Chadwick found the neutron, each changing the model.

points.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
points.brief: The atomic number is the number of protons. Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

points.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
points.brief: Unstable nuclei decay by giving off alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays until they become stable. Each goes a different distance through matter.

points.title: Half-life and radiocarbon dating
points.brief: Half-life is the time for half the unstable atoms in a sample to decay. Carbon-14 dating uses it to find the age of once-living things, including evidence of First Peoples in Australia.

points.title: Reactants and products
points.brief: In a reaction, the starting substances are the reactants and the new ones are the products. A word equation names them with an arrow between.

points.title: Conservation of mass
points.brief: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction, never made or lost, so the total mass stays the same. In an open container a gas may escape and seem to lose mass.

points.title: Balancing a chemical equation
points.brief: A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides, adjusted with numbers in front of formulas, never by changing the formulas.

units.title: Science as a human endeavour and inquiry

chapters.title: How science is checked and used

points.title: Peer review and publication
points.brief: Scientists publish their methods and results so other experts can check them before publication and repeat them after, which is how knowledge is validated.

points.title: Science, technology and engineering
points.brief: New technology lets science find out more, such as better telescopes, and new science leads to new technology, such as medical imaging.

points.title: Why society takes up new science
points.brief: Cost, evidence, trust, government support and culture affect whether people adopt a practice, such as solar panels or recycling.

points.title: What gets researched
points.brief: Society's needs and values steer which research gets funded, such as cutting greenhouse gases or treating common diseases.

points.title: Validity
points.brief: An investigation is valid when it tests what it set out to test, which needs controlled variables and a fair method.

points.title: Reproducibility and replicability
points.brief: Results are replicable when the same person gets similar results again, and reproducible when others using the same method get them too.

points.title: Random and systematic errors
points.brief: Random errors scatter results either side of the true value and are reduced by repeats. Systematic errors push every result the same way, such as a scale not set to zero.

points.title: Mean, median and range
points.brief: The mean is the total divided by the number of results, the median is the middle result, and the range is the largest minus the smallest.
